title: Gottfried Leibniz and the Binary Number System (1703)
explainer: The German mathematician Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz, who had worked out the idea decades earlier, published a full description of the binary number system — numbers written with only the digits 0 and 1 — in a 1703 paper, after a Jesuit missionary in China showed him how the I Ching's hexagrams could be read as binary patterns. Leibniz treated binary purely as a mathematical curiosity useful for number theory; there was no electronics yet to apply it to, and it took more than two centuries before anyone connected 'two symbols' to 'two voltage states' and built a machine around it. That gap matters: the base-2 positional system you converted 173 into above is centuries older than any computer, and was motivated by pure arithmetic, not circuitry.

title: The Invention of the Transistor at Bell Labs (1947)
explainer: On December 16, 1947, Bell Labs physicists John Bardeen and Walter Brattain built the first working point-contact transistor — a solid-state device that can amplify or switch an electrical signal without the bulk, fragility, and warm-up delay of a vacuum tube; William Shockley, who led the research group, soon developed a more practical junction design, and the three shared the 1956 Nobel Prize in Physics. This is the physical, hardware-side reason the AND/OR/NOT/XOR gates you just built truth tables for exist as real circuits at all: each gate is a small arrangement of transistors wired so that high and low voltages on the inputs force a predictable high or low voltage on the output. A modern CPU is billions of that same 1947 device, shrunk down and wired together to implement exactly those same four operations.
